deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is part of Riemann's physiological-acoustical fragment on the mechanics of the middle ear, published posthumously by Henle in 1867 as "Mechanik des Ohres" and reprinted in the Gesammelte Werke. Section IV sets out to find how the ossicles must shift when the outside temperature falls so that all contact surfaces still fit exactly. The previous page established the physical premise: on cooling, the small ossicles cool and contract much more than the walls of the tympanic cavity, which stay nearly unchanged.

The argument on this page is purely qualitative and geometric.

(1) Fixed reference. The incus–tympanic joint is taken as the part of the ossicular chain most rigidly tied to the cavity wall. It is effectively fixed: the short process of the incus rests on the wall.

(2) First consequence. Every distance inside a solid body shrinks on cooling. So the distance from the incus–stapes joint to this articular surface shrinks, i.e. the long process of the incus effectively shortens. The consequence is drawn on the next page.

(3) A second nearly fixed point. On the malleus, the upper end of the manubrium is the part that is presumably least displaceable, at least parallel to the tympanic ring, because it is held in the membrane.

(4) The triangle. Call A the incus–tympanic joint, B the upper manubrium point fixed in the membrane, and C the incus–malleus joint.
- Side c = |AB| belongs to the wall/membrane frame and stays nearly unchanged.
- Sides a = |CB| and b = |CA| run through bone, so both decrease (completed on the next page).
- Hence the angle γ at C between CA and CB must open slightly.

(5) Justification (my addition). By the law of cosines, cos γ = (a^2 + b^2 − c^2)/(2ab). Scale a and b by λ < 1 and keep c fixed:
 cos γ(λ) = (a^2 + b^2)/(2ab) − c^2/(2 λ^2 a b).
This is increasing in λ. So when λ decreases, cos γ decreases and γ increases.
More generally, shrinking both legs while keeping the opposite side fixed always widens the included angle.

The next page turns this into small rotations of the malleus and a motion of its long process in the Glaserian fissure.
errors: No mathematical error. The steps rest on physical idealisations that Riemann himself flags as conjectural ('wahrscheinlich'): that the walls and the membrane points are fixed, and that the bone contracts uniformly (isotropically).

The angle conclusion strictly needs |AB| constant, or shrinking proportionally less than the bony sides. The text says only 'nahezu ungeändert' (nearly unchanged). That suffices, since by the previous page the bone contracts much more than the wall.

results.what: On cooling, the angle at the incus–malleus joint between the lines to the incus–tympanic joint and to the fixed manubrium point opens, because the two bony sides shrink while the third side (in the wall/membrane frame) stays fixed.
results.modern_name: Law of cosines monotonicity (included angle increases when adjacent sides shrink with the opposite side fixed); kinematic thermal-compatibility argument
results.usually_credited_to: Elementary geometry; the application is Riemann's own, in 'Mechanik des Ohres' (published by Henle, 1867)

results.what: Differential thermal contraction of the ossicles relative to the tympanic wall as a reason for adjustable joints and self-adjusting ossicle positions.
results.modern_name: Thermal compatibility / differential thermal expansion in a linked mechanism

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to Riemann's known and published ear-mechanics fragment (Henle 1867; Gesammelte Werke). The geometry is elementary triangle reasoning. Nothing here is new or unattributed.

checkable.asserts: d(cos gamma)/d(lambda) = c^2/(lambda^3 a b) > 0, so shrinking both sides (lambda<1) lowers cos gamma and widens the angle at C.
Numerical example: the 3-4-5 triangle with legs scaled by 0.9 and hypotenuse fixed at 5 has a larger angle at C than 90 degrees (cos goes from 0 to a negative value).

transcription_corrections: Line 1: the struck word 'alle' is correctly shown as deleted. 'bestim-ten' is written 'bestimm-ten', with a correction over the 'mm'.
'nahezu[?] ungeändert' — the image supports 'nahezu ungeändert'; the question mark can be dropped.
Minor orthography: Riemann writes 'Ambos' (not 'Amboß') on this page; the transcription is consistent with the image.
